a.entradas.disco-alado.titulo_alternativ: The winged disk, symbol of Nibiru or of a spacecraft
a.entradas.disco-alado.interpretacion: Sitchin identifies the winged sun disk, found in Egypt, in Assyria (with the god Ashur or Shamash inside) and in Persia (the faravahar), as the emblem of Nibiru, the "planet of the crossing", which is shown with wings because it travels across the sky. On ancient astronaut television, the winged disk with a human figure is also presented as a spacecraft or as a pilot in his vehicle.
a.entradas.disco-alado.afirmaciones.0.af: Sitchin: the winged disk represents the planet Nibiru.
a.entradas.disco-alado.afirmaciones.0.re: The winged disk is a solar motif of Egyptian origin (Behdety, Horus of Edfu) that spread throughout the Near East in the 2nd millennium BC. In Assyria it is associated with Shamash or Ashur as a symbol of divine protection of kingship. No text links it with Nibiru, and on kudurrus Shamash's symbol is the star disk, while Marduk is represented by the spade (marru).
a.entradas.disco-alado.afirmaciones.0.fu: J. Black and A. Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia, 1992; Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com
a.entradas.disco-alado.afirmaciones.1.af: Ancient Aliens: the human figure inside the disk is a pilot in his spacecraft.
a.entradas.disco-alado.afirmaciones.1.re: In Neo-Assyrian art the figure in the disk imitates the king's posture and weapons (the bow) and symbolizes the protective god who accompanies the monarch in battle. It is an iconographic convention that evolved over centuries, not the depiction of a vehicle.
a.entradas.disco-alado.veredicto: The winged disk is a solar symbol and a symbol of royal protection with a well-studied iconographic history; its identification with Nibiru or with a spacecraft has no support in the sources.
a.entradas.lamassu.titulo_alternativo: The winged beings: Anunnaki or hybrids
a.entradas.lamassu.interpretacion: Ancient Aliens presents the Assyrian reliefs of winged beings (lamassu, winged spirits and bird-headed figures) as depictions of the Anunnaki or of hybrids they created, and as proof that the Mesopotamians lived alongside nonhuman beings.
a.entradas.lamassu.afirmaciones.0.afirma: Ancient Aliens: the Babylonian and Assyrian winged men are Anunnaki, and the bird-headed figure is another Anunnaki.
a.entradas.lamassu.afirmaciones.0.replic: The winged men are Neo-Assyrian protective spirits (lamassu and apkallu), and the bird-headed figure is a griffin-demon. None is linked to the Anunnaki. The human-headed winged bulls guarded palace gateways, and their protective function appears in the Assyrian rituals themselves.
a.entradas.lamassu.afirmaciones.0.fuente: Jason Colavito, review of Ancient Aliens S6E03; F. A. M. Wiggermann, Mesopotamian Protective Spirits, 1992
a.entradas.lamassu.veredicto: The lamassu and winged spirits are apotropaic figures of Assyrian art; the series strips them of their ritual context.
a.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.interpr: Sitchin maintains that the Sumerians knew of planets invisible to the naked eye (Uranus, Neptune and Pluto), their colors and sizes, the precession of the equinoxes and a system of twelve bodies, and that only a spacefaring civilization could have passed on that knowledge. Sitchin (Genesis Revisited, 1990) presented the Voyager 2 probe's arrival at Uranus and Neptune as confirmation of the Sumerian descriptions. Temple attributes knowledge about Sirius to the same source.
a.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.afirmac: Sitchin: the Sumerians knew of twelve bodies in the solar system, including Uranus, Neptune and Pluto.

The cuneiform astronomical texts, such as MUL.APIN and the Astronomical Diaries, mention only five planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn), plus the Sun and the Moon. Babylonian mathematical astronomy, highly refined, dates mostly to the 1st millennium BC and developed out of centuries of systematic naked-eye observation. Heiser points out that Sitchin's equivalences between gods and planets do not match the scribes' astronomical lists.
H. Hunger and D. Pingree, MUL.APIN: An Astronomical Compendium in Cuneiform, 1989; Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com
Sitchin: the period of 3,600 years and the use of the number 12 reflect received cosmic knowledge.

3,600 and 12 are natural numbers in a sexagesimal system (60², divisors of 60), which also served for the lunisolar calendar of twelve months. Their importance is arithmetical and calendrical, not the trace of an unknown planet.
O. Neugebauer, The Exact Sciences in Antiquity, 1957
a.entradas.astronomia-babilonica.veredic: Babylonian astronomy is an extraordinary and well-documented human achievement; the knowledge of outer planets attributed to it does not appear in its texts.
a.entradas.an-anu.interpretacion: Sitchin makes Anu the sovereign who reigns on Nibiru and visits the Earth on rare occasions; his "heaven" would be the planet itself. The King List and the myths that place him at the top of the pantheon would reflect the colony's political hierarchy, and the formula "kingship came down from heaven" would mean that it came from Nibiru.
a.entradas.an-anu.afirmaciones.0.afirmac: Sitchin: Anu's heaven is the planet Nibiru.
a.entradas.an-anu.afirmaciones.0.replica: An means "sky" and is both the god and the vault of heaven, the highest level of Mesopotamian cosmology. In the texts Nibiru is associated with Marduk and Jupiter, not with Anu, and no text identifies Anu's heaven with a planet.
a.entradas.an-anu.afirmaciones.0.fuente_: W. Horowitz, Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography, 1998; Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com
a.entradas.an-anu.veredicto: Anu is the god of the sky and father of the gods; his conversion into a planetary monarch is a reading by Sitchin with no textual support.
a.entradas.enlil.interpretacion: For Sitchin, Enlil is the commander-in-chief of the Anunnaki on Earth, brother and rival of Enki, who directs operations from the control center at Nippur (Duranki). His hostility toward humans, for example in decreeing the Flood, would be a political decision within a dynastic dispute between the branches of Enlil and Enki.
a.entradas.enlil.afirmaciones.0.afirmaci: Sitchin: Enlil and Enki are half brothers of an extraterrestrial dynasty at odds over the succession.
a.entradas.enlil.afirmaciones.0.replica: In Mesopotamian theology Enlil is the god of air and of authority, king of the gods with his seat at Nippur, and his relationship with Enki varies from text to text. Rivalries between gods are common narrative and theological devices, and the control center and succession laws Sitchin describes do not appear in any source.
a.entradas.enlil.afirmaciones.0.fuente_r: Black and Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia, 1992
a.entradas.enlil.veredicto: Enlil is the great god of Nippur; the role of mission commander is a narrative creation of Sitchin's.
a.entradas.enki-ea.titulo_alternativo: Enki, the chief scientist and lord of the mines
a.entradas.enki-ea.interpretacion: Enki is the hero of Sitchin's saga: the first Anunnaki to splash down in the Persian Gulf, founder of Eridu, engineer of the African gold mines, creator of humankind together with Ninhursag and protector of humanity against Enlil. In The Lost Book of Enki (2001), Sitchin writes Enki's supposed memoirs in the first person. For Tellinger, southern Africa was Enki's mining domain, and in Parks Enki is a leading figure among the Gina'abul.
a.entradas.enki-ea.afirmaciones.0.afirma: Sitchin: Enki was an Anunnaki who ran the gold mines of southern Africa (the Abzu).
a.entradas.enki-ea.afirmaciones.0.replic: The Abzu is the underground freshwater ocean and the seat of Enki's temple at Eridu, not a mining region in Africa. Colavito considers Ea's membership among the Anunnaki to be Sitchin's invention. The Lost Book of Enki translates no tablet: it is a novel by Sitchin himself.
a.entradas.enki-ea.afirmaciones.0.fuente: Jason Colavito, review of Ancient Aliens S6E03; Black and Green, 1992
a.entradas.enki-ea.veredicto: Enki/Ea is the god of fresh waters, wisdom and magic; his role as genetic engineer and miner comes from Sitchin, not from the texts.
a.entradas.inanna-ishtar.interpretacion: Sitchin presents Inanna/Ishtar as an aviator who travels the skies in her "sky chamber" (MU). He believes he sees her depicted with a helmet, goggles and headphones in a statuette from Mari and in reliefs where she wears headdresses and objects hanging from her chest. Her political ambition and her travels between cities would be those of an influential Anunnaki.
Sitchin: Inanna's iconography shows a pilot's helmet and flight equipment.

Heiser shows that the images Sitchin cites depict horned headdresses, the mark of divinity, and ceremonial necklaces or counterweights. MU does not mean "spacecraft", and the "sky chamber" depends on that mistaken translation.
a.entradas.inanna-ishtar.veredicto: Inanna is the goddess of love, war and the planet Venus; her characterization as a pilot comes from a literal reading of ritual images.
a.entradas.ninhursag.interpretacion: For Sitchin, Ninhursag (Ninmah, Ninti, Mammi) is the medical officer of the Anunnaki and the biological "mother" of the first human being: she would have carried or implanted the embryos of the Adamu. Her title of "mother of the gods" and midwife of humankind would describe a technical function.
a.entradas.ninhursag.afirmaciones.0.afir: Sitchin: Ninhursag carried the first human by means of an embryo-implantation technique.
a.entradas.ninhursag.afirmaciones.0.repl: Ninhursag is the mother goddess and goddess of the mountains. In Atrahasis, as Mami/Nintu, she presides over the mythical birth with the fourteen womb goddesses, a reflection of midwifery practices, not of laboratory procedures. Her symbol is the omega, which possibly represents a uterus or a midwife's instrument.
a.entradas.ninhursag.afirmaciones.0.fuen: Lambert and Millard, 1969; Black and Green, 1992
a.entradas.ninhursag.veredicto: Ninhursag is a mother goddess with functions of fertility and childbirth; her role as a medical scientist is a modern reinterpretation.
a.entradas.utu-shamash.interpretacion: In The Stairway to Heaven (1980), Sitchin makes Utu/Shamash the officer in charge of the Anunnaki's post-Flood spaceport, located on the Sinai Peninsula, and of the landing platform at Baalbek. His "eagles" would be the astronauts under his command, and the depictions of eagle-headed beings, helmeted pilots.
a.entradas.utu-shamash.afirmaciones.0.af: Sitchin: Shamash ran a spaceport in Sinai.
a.entradas.utu-shamash.afirmaciones.0.re: Shamash is the god of the Sun and of justice, worshiped at Sippar and Larsa. No Mesopotamian text mentions a spaceport or places him in Sinai. The bird-headed figures are protective griffin-demons of Assyrian art.
a.entradas.utu-shamash.veredicto: Utu/Shamash is the sun god and judge; the Sinai spaceport is Sitchin's construction.
a.entradas.nanna-sin.titulo_alternativo: Nanna and the nuclear fall of Ur
a.entradas.nanna-sin.interpretacion: Sitchin (The Wars of Gods and Men, 1985) interprets the laments in which Nanna/Sin, the moon god and patron of Ur, mourns the destruction of his city as a god's testimony to the radioactive cloud of the nuclear war among the Anunnaki in 2024 BC.
a.entradas.nanna-sin.afirmaciones.0.afir: Sitchin: Nanna's grief for Ur describes the radioactive contamination of the city.
a.entradas.nanna-sin.afirmaciones.0.repl: The Lament for the Destruction of Ur belongs to a liturgical genre that attributes political ruin, the Elamite invasion at the end of Ur III, to the decision of the gods. The "wind" is a metaphor for divine wrath. Ur was rebuilt and remained inhabited for centuries, which is incompatible with radioactive contamination.
a.entradas.nanna-sin.afirmaciones.0.fuen: P. Michalowski, The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur, 1989
a.entradas.nanna-sin.veredicto: Nanna/Sin is the god of the Moon; the nuclear reading of the laments has no archaeological or philological support.
a.entradas.marduk.titulo_alternativo: Marduk, the planet and the god
a.entradas.marduk.interpretacion: Sitchin takes Marduk to be two things at once: the Babylonian name of the planet Nibiru in the Enuma Elish and a specific Anunnaki, son of Enki, who supposedly contested power with Enlil's branch and proclaimed himself supreme god in Babylon. He also identifies him with the Egyptian Ra. His rise in the 2nd millennium BC would be the outcome of the wars of the gods.
a.entradas.marduk.afirmaciones.0.afirmac: Sitchin: Marduk is the planet Nibiru and at the same time the Anunnaki Ra of Egypt.
a.entradas.marduk.afirmaciones.0.replica: Marduk's rise reflects the political importance of Babylon from Hammurabi onward and, above all, in the Kassite period and under Nebuchadnezzar I. His star is Nēberu/Jupiter in Babylonian astronomy. Colavito notes that in the Enuma Elish Marduk is not an Anunnaki. The identification with Ra has no basis in Egyptian or Mesopotamian texts.
a.entradas.marduk.afirmaciones.0.fuente_: Jason Colavito, review of Ancient Aliens S6E03; W. G. Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths, 2013
a.entradas.marduk.veredicto: Marduk is the god of Babylon, whose exaltation has documented political causes; his identification with a wandering planet comes from Sitchin.
a.entradas.tiamat.interpretacion: For Sitchin, Tiamat was a watery planet located between Mars and Jupiter. One of Nibiru's "satellite-winds" split it: one half formed the Earth, which inherited its oceans, and the other the asteroid belt. This is also how he explains the abundance of water on Earth. Alford (When the Gods Came Down, 2000) in turn proposed that the myths recall the explosion of a planet.
a.entradas.tiamat.afirmaciones.0.afirmac: Sitchin: Tiamat was a planet whose remains form the Earth and the asteroid belt.
a.entradas.tiamat.afirmaciones.0.replica: In Akkadian, Tiamat means "sea" (tâmtu), the primordial salt sea. The total mass of the asteroid belt amounts to a small percentage of the Moon's mass, far from that of an Earth-sized planet. Earth's water is explained by the planet's formation and by the delivery of icy bodies.
a.entradas.tiamat.afirmaciones.0.fuente_: W. G. Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths, 2013; Peter James (cited in "Zecharia Sitchin", Wikipedia)
a.entradas.tiamat.veredicto: Tiamat is the personification of the primordial sea; her planetary reading contradicts both the text and astronomy.
a.entradas.apsu.interpretacion: In Sitchin's cosmogony, Apsu, "he who existed from the beginning", is the Sun, and his union with Tiamat describes the formation of the solar system. Mummu, his adviser, would be Mercury.
a.entradas.apsu.afirmaciones.0.replica: Apsu (Sumerian abzu) is the underground reservoir of fresh water, the domain of Enki, and his temple at Eridu was called é-abzu. Peter James uses this identification as an example of how Sitchin distorts the texts.
a.entradas.apsu.afirmaciones.0.fuente_re: Peter James (cited in "Zecharia Sitchin", Wikipedia); W. Horowitz, Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography, 1998
a.entradas.apsu.veredicto: Apsu is the underground freshwater ocean; the equivalence with the Sun has no textual support.
